title: Binary Tree Right Side View
description: Brute force to optimized: full level order traversal versus recording only the last node of each BFS round.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from that side, ordered from top to bottom.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","One value per level, the rightmost visible node at that level"],["Key Insight","The rightmost node of every level is exactly the node visible from the right side at that level"],["Constraints","Up to 100 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Visible from the right side, level by level\"","A level-order BFS where only the LAST node processed per level needs to be recorded"]]}

blocks.text: Standing to the right of the tree, at every level the FIRST node your eye reaches (blocked by nothing to its right) is the rightmost node of that level; everything to its left at the same level is hidden behind it. So the answer is simply the rightmost node's value from each level, collected top to bottom.

blocks.title: Analogy: Looking at a Row of Buildings From the Side
blocks.text: Picture looking at a skyline from the right side, one row (floor) at a time; from that vantage point, only the building furthest to the right on each floor is visible, since it blocks the view of anything behind it on that same floor.

blocks.caption: The rightmost node at every level is exactly the one visible from the right side

blocks.text: Result: [1,3,4]. Level 0 has just 1. Level 1's rightmost is 3. Level 2's rightmost is 4 (even though 5 is also on level 2, on the left side).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A standard level-order BFS visits every level's nodes, in left-to-right order within each level.

Observation 2: The LAST node processed within a level's round (in a left-to-right BFS) is exactly that level's rightmost node.

Observation 3: Instead of collecting an entire level's values and taking the last one afterward, the algorithm can directly record only the last node's value seen in each round, avoiding storing the full level unnecessarily.
This leads to a level-order BFS, per level directly recording only the LAST node processed in that round.
Perform a full level order traversal, collecting every level's complete list of values, then take the last element of each completed level.
Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting full levels and extracting the last value afterward implements the definition in two clear steps.
This stores every node's value even though only the rightmost one per level is ever used, wasting space that a direct approach avoids.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for storing every level's full contents.
Limitation: recording only the last node of each round directly, during the BFS itself, avoids storing every level's full contents.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Run a standard level-order BFS. At the start of each round, note the current queue size (this round's level size). Process exactly that many nodes; for the VERY LAST one processed in this round, record its value directly into the result (instead of building a full level list and extracting the last element afterward).
Use a level-order BFS, directly recording only the last node processed in each round.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Round (level)","Nodes processed left to right","Recorded value"],"rows":[["0","1","1"],["1","2, 3","3 (the last one)"],["2","5, 4","4 (the last one)"]]}

blocks.text: Since the BFS processes each level's nodes strictly left to right, the last node dequeued within a given round is guaranteed to be that level's rightmost node, exactly the one visible from the right side; recording it directly during the traversal (rather than after building a full level list) is correct and avoids unnecessary storage.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the queue in the worst case (a wide tree), O(1) extra beyond that for the result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Full level order, extract last afterward","O(n)","O(n) for every level's full contents","Correct, but stores unnecessary data."],["BFS, record only the last node per round","O(n)","O(n) for the queue only","The expected, direct solution."]]}

blocks.text: Binary Tree Right Side View is a direct, minimal variant of level-order BFS: recognizing that only the LAST node of each round matters avoids unnecessary storage.

items: Using the FIRST node of each round instead of the last, which would give the LEFT side view instead of the right side view.
Building and storing entire level lists when only the last value of each is ever actually needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty tree","Returns an empty list."],["A tree that is entirely a left-leaning chain","Every level still has exactly one node, so that single node is \"visible\" from the right at each level."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "the last node processed in each BFS round is the rightmost node of that level" clarifies the key insight cleanly and quickly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "what would you see looking at the tree from one side", think: level-order BFS, recording the first or last node of each round depending on which side.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(n) time; recording only the last node per round directly avoids the brute force's unnecessary O(n) storage of full level contents.

items: Pattern: level-order BFS, recording only the last node of each round.
Core Idea: the rightmost node of every level is exactly the node visible from the right side at that level.
Space: O(n) for storing full levels in the brute force, O(n) for just the queue in the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the last-processed node in a left-to-right BFS round is the rightmost node of that level.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, quick BFS variant problem.
One line memory trick: last node of every round.
